records.our_prose: Kohlrabi is a moderate feeder that wants steady, even growth rather than a late surge. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Iowa State: 1 to 2 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting or thinning, when the plants are roughly 4 inches tall (Utah State: about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row). Keep nitrogen and water even through bulbing, since both a stall and a late flush hurt texture; avoid heavy late nitrogen, which can grow leaves at the expense of a clean bulb.
source_names: Texas A&M AgriLife -- Fall Vegetable Gardening Guide

records.our_prose: The bulb reaches about 2 to 3 inches in diameter (larger for the giant storage types), firm and smooth, before it turns woody.
records.source_context: Harvest & Storage Kohlrabi is typically ready to harvest 50-60 days after sowing seed in the garden, depending on the cultivar. Harvest kohlrabi when the thickened stems are 2 to 3 inches in diameter. (Kohlrabi larger than 3 inches in diameter will be tough, woody, and bitter.) Simply pull the entire plant from the ground and remove the leaves and roots.

records.our_prose: Kohlrabi is ready when the swollen stem reaches about 2 to 3 inches in diameter for standard types, the size of a tennis ball, firm and smooth. Cut the bulb off at the base while it is young; past about 3 inches standard cultivars turn tough, woody, and bitter and do not recover. Giant storage types (Kossak, Superschmelz) stay tender at a much larger size. Trim the leafy tops and refrigerate promptly.

records.our_prose: Kohlrabi is quick to grow and does well both in spring and fall here, but the fall crop has the edge: the swollen stem stays mild and tender in cool weather instead of turning woody the way summer heat pushes it. Sow in late winter to early spring for a spring crop, then sow again in mid-to-late summer for fall.

records.our_prose: In the Willamette Valley and around Puget Sound, sow kohlrabi seed directly in the garden in April for an early-summer bulb, then sow again in mid-July for a fall crop, which is often the sweeter of the two. On the immediate coast, hold off until July; the cool, foggy coastal spring is not the time for this one there, but a July-and-August sowing still gives you two rounds of bulbs before the mild fall frost arrives. Pick bulbs about tennis-ball size, before they turn woody.

records.our_prose: USU Extension's St. George planting chart sets kohlrabi in the Group A (Hardy) band, transplants out about February 15, seed started indoors roughly four weeks earlier. The stem swells to harvest size in about 55 days, but cutting is capped by the end of April: St. George reaches 100°F in June, July, and August, and the stem turns woody and pithy well before that. By analogy to USU's fall-gardening guidance for the St. George area, which sows the quick cole crops and greens from mid-July into mid-August, a second round of seedlings goes in indoors around mid-to-late June for a fall harvest running into early October ahead of the November 1 average first frost.

records.our_prose: Work plenty of compost into a loose, fertile, well-drained bed before planting, and mix in a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10. Loosen any compaction, since kohlrabi wants steady, unchecked growth for a tender bulb, and aim the pH at about 6.0 to 7.0, liming acidic ground where clubroot is a concern.

records.our_prose: Kohlrabi is grown both ways. Direct sowing is simple and common since the crop is fast: sow 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep once the soil is workable and thin to 6 to 9 inches apart. For an earlier or more uniform crop, start transplants indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and plant them out 1 to 2 weeks before the last frost, since young plants take light frost. Avoid exposing young plants to a long cold spell (more than about a week of nights below roughly 45 to 50°F), which can trigger bolting. Sow the fall crop in mid-summer. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.
records.source_context: Incorporate some organic matter and a complete fertilizer into the area before planting. Plant seeds ¼-½ inch deep, 1-2 weeks before the last frost in the spring. Thin seedlings or transplant kohlrabi 6 inches apart in the row with rows 1 foot apart.
